The meeting, the ministerial meeting of the Peacebuilding Commission is called to order. Ladies and gentlemen, it is with a deep sense of honor that I wish to welcome you to this ministerial meeting under the theme of national ownership and practice, strengthening inclusive state institutions through international peacebuilding support. By meeting today on the margins of the high-level week of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in order to consider the crucial importance of national ownership in the realm of peacebuilding, insofar as a peace that is not rooted in national priorities cannot withstand the test of time. Today's meeting is an important opportunity to consider how international support for peacebuilding can be built on the basis of priorities set out at the national level, can strengthen inclusive and accountable institutions, and support without ever substituting to support member states in the establishment and the sustaining of peace. I wish to thank you for your presence and to welcome our distinguished briefers whose presence honors us. Her Excellency, my sister, Amina Mohammed, Deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations; my brother, Musalia Mudavadi, Prime Cabinet Secretary of the Republic of Kenya; His Excellency, the Foreign Minister of Papua Guinea, and of course, Her Excellency, Madame Marie-Laure Akin Olugbade, Principal Vice President of the African Development Bank. Twenty years after its inception, the PBC is at a turning point. The Pact for the Future reaffirmed the centrality of peacebuilding within the international peace and security agenda, the 2025 review of the peacebuilding architecture encourages us to transform the lessons learned into operational guidance. Peacebuilding, by its definition, constitutes an initiative that is undertaken over the long term. Peacebuilding requires that our tools evolve to reflect varying contexts, but especially for them to remain rooted in a fundamental conviction, the conviction that a lasting peace cannot be built in the place of states and societies. In this vein, I wish to share with you six considerations that can guide our discussion today. First and foremost, national ownership must never become merely a principle, a rhetorical principle. National ownership must not be boiled down to validation after the fact of programs and agendas designed from abroad. Peace cannot be imported. Peace is built from within. International support can be effective when it addresses national demand and supports priorities set out in an independent manner and strengthens the abilities of a state rather than substituting said state. This includes gradually transitioning from an approach of assistance to that of partnership based upon shared responsibility, respect for sovereignty and preparation from with once missions withdraw, respect for independence of national Second, national ownership is necessarily multidimensional. It is political, first and foremost. States need to be able to set out their own national priorities through inclusive processes, bringing together local authorities, women, youth, and civil society. And they need to be capacities to plan, implement, assess, and be held accountable for policies and financial support. At the financial level, states cannot genuinely steer their peacebuilding strategies if they remain dependent permanently upon ad hoc, unpredictable financing. These three dimensions are inextricably linked. Political ownership without institutional ownership remains a mere ambition and institutional capacity without ownership is also tenuous. So strengthening national institutions represents a direct investment in peace. Legitimate, inclusive, responsible institutions that can prevent to provide services to their citizens represent the best guarantee against relapse into crisis. In this vein, we have set out an integrated approach of the peace, security, development governance nexus, as was stressed by His Majesty the King Mohammed VI in the extraordinary summit during the extraordinary summit of the African Union, which was held last August in Luanda, Morocco has made peace, security, and stability in Africa a strategic choice, a longstanding consistent commitment through its contribution to conflict prevention, to mediation, to peacekeeping, peacebuilding, as well as post-conflict recovery," end of quote. This philosophy guides our efforts in the Central African Republic, where Morocco has the honor of chairing the peacebuilding configuration the country configuration. This has been the case since 2014 by providing support for the priorities that have been set out by the Central African authorities. Fourth consideration, a commission that supports national ownership itself needs to be present more present on the ground for this reason, we propose a greater focus on outside the walls, so to speak, PBC efforts. Peacebuilding cannot be considered in New York alone. There need to be regular sessions organized with countries concerned, which allow the Commission to engage in direct dialogue with governments. local bodies, economic stakeholders, and civil society. And this specifically allows for international decision-making to be brought closer to those who shoulder on a day-to-day basis responsibility for peace. In the same vein, we propose consideration of the feasibility of developing with national authorities a model for national ownership diagnosis. And under no circumstances does this imply an assessment of states and the basis of the yardstick of standards set out from abroad, but rather to identify with the states the necessary capacity in order to shape, steer, absorb, and sustain peacebuilding initiatives. Fifth consideration, national ownership requires true financial predictability. The Peacebuilding Fund remains an important catalyst, but the magnitude and the duration of the needs requires far broader mobilization. The Commission needs to strengthen partnerships with international financial institutions, regional development banks, national development banks, as well as other financial partners, so as to ensure that the financing for peace investments and development, for these to be mutually reinforcing around national priorities. There can be no lasting ownership when priorities when priorities are national, but the means for the achievement of these priorities are unpredictable. Sixth consideration, the value added of the Commission lies in its ability to build bridges, bridges between peace and development, bridges between states and the multilateral system, between national priorities and international resources, but also between the various bodies of the United Nations. Experience in Morocco at the helm of the Central African configuration, demonstrated this specifically through the advice conveyed to the Security Council in close coordination with the Central African authorities ahead of the renewal of MINUSCA's mandate. The PBC can neither substitute for states nor replicate the work of other institutions. Its strength specifically lies in the ability to bring parties together to provide support and to establish conditions for national institutions to take over the reins. After 20 years of experience, ladies and gentlemen, our ambition must not be solely limited to making more of peacebuilding, but rather to achieving better, to doing so better. And there needs to be a focus on peace building as a key pillar for the UN peace architecture with an approach with an emphasis on empowerment, ownership, and transitions that are implemented by national authorities. In this spirit, we, in our capacity as chair of the PBC, will continue to work towards the 2025 review and to strengthen this institution for the advancement of a genuinely national, inclusive, and sustainable peace. Thank you. It is my pleasure, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, to to give the floor to our distinguished high-level speakers, and it is now my pleasure to invite Her Excellency Amina Mohamed, Deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations, to deliver her remarks.

Your Excellency, Mr. Nassir Bourita, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation, and Moroccan Expatriates of the Kingdom of Morocco, and our Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Minister Bourita, thank you for bringing us together and for Morocco's leadership of this commission in these times. Sustaining peace rests to a great extent on trust between people and the state. That if they are wronged, someone will listen. That if their child falls ill, someone will give them the medical care they have a right to. That a dispute over land will be settled in a courtroom rather than by force. That is a social contract, and when it is torn up, conflict is rarely behind it. Keeping it is the first responsibility of any government, and the job of partners like us is to help them keep it well through the institutions that people rely on every day. An agreement can end a war in a day. Peace takes much longer. It grows slowly, as institutions start to work, as services reach people again, as trust is restored. In June, the Secretary General reminded this commission that it was created to nurture the seeds of peace long enough for them to take root. Institutions are those roots, and helping countries grow them is what makes this commission's work between peace and development so valuable. Last year's review of the peace building architecture was very clear about who leads. Countries bear the primary responsibility for preventing conflict and building peace, and the rest of us are there to back the priorities that they set when they ask for our support. We know what happens when that balance is right. Liberia moved from a peacekeeping mission to a peacebuilding strategy of its own, with this Commission alongside it. The Central African Republic, with the Commission's support, restored state authority and held its first local election in decades. Colombia kept the world's attention on the priorities that it set itself and on women, young people, indigenous communities who lived through the conflict. Ownership, as this commission frames it, covers who sets the priorities, whether institutions can deliver on them, and whether the money flows through a country's own systems where citizens can see how it is spent. And crucially, women belong in all three. The research shows that peace agreements last longer when women help shape them. The institutions that come afterwards are no different. A justice system women trust, a police service women are part of to give the social contract meaning for women and girls and make it stronger for everyone. So I would urge every partner here to bring women into the design of our support from the beginning and not as an afterthought, and to put money directly into women's organizations. They are often the ones keeping communities together long before any national strategy is written. Excellencies, national strategies are how countries bring all of this together, and Sao Tome and Principe offer a good example. They developed a national prevention strategy with support from the Peacebuilding Fund and brought it to this Commission, and I congratulate them. Delivering it will take years, and it will need partners who will stay the course. The Peacebuilding Fund is very good at the first step. It moves early. It takes calculated risks while using its funding to get things started. Keeping them going needs patient, long-term finance from our development banks, our financial institutions, and the private sector. I am very pleased that the African Development Bank is with us today and that our partnership with the bank keeps growing. We also need to be able to show what works. The new UN system data commons and the peacebuilding impact hub are helping us to learn from experience and improve what we offer countries. Let me end my remarks by saying this: roots grow slowly. The countries in this room are doing that patient work every day, strengthening courts and police services, getting services back to communities, bringing women and young people into the decisions that shape their future and rebuilding, little by little, the trust between people and the state. They deserve strong partners who show the same patience. The United Nations and the Peacebuilding Support Fund, led by ASG Elizabeth Sverha, intend to be that kind of partner and will be with you every step of the way. I thank you.

Mr. Chair, Madam Deputy Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I thank His Excellency Nasser Bourita, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Morocco, for his stewardship of the Peacebuilding Commission, and I commend the peacebuilding support Office for advancing the implementation of the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review resolutions, as well as the successful convening of the inaugural Peacebuilding Week. Kenya welcomed the progress made through the General Assembly resolutions 76/305 and 78/257, which have strengthened the foundation for more predictable financing for prevention and peacebuilding. For Kenya, prevention endures when it is anchored in national institutions informed by communities and aligned with development priorities. International solidarity is most effective when it reinforces national capacity rather than replacing it. Allow me to offer five brief reflections from Kenya's experience and our engagement with the Commission. First, national ownership must be inclusive. Partners add greatest value when they support nationally identified priorities and wide and meaningful participation by women, youth, civil society, and local communities. In Kenya, many durable peace-building gains have grown from communities themselves. International support should strengthen national systems and allow for continuity long after external programs have ended. Second, institution building works best when support is channeled through national systems, not around them. joint analysis, predictable financing, and technical assistance to transfer knowledge and responsibility and confidence to national institutions over time. Kenya's Uyuano Platform for Peace demonstrates this approach by linking community, knowledge, peace committees, and formal state institutions for mediation, dialogue, early warning, and early response. Third, the Peacebuilding Commission has a unique convening role at the intersection of peace, development, and finance. It can bring governments, development partners, financial institutions, and private investors around nationally identified priorities. Kenya, therefore, proposes a peace-building peer learning platform under the commission to facilitate practical exchanges of lessons from nationally led prevention efforts and strengthen the link between peace-building fund investments and wider development financing. Fourth, peacebuilding support delivers the greatest impact when it's demand-driven, flexible, and rooted in national realities. Across regions, experience increasingly shows that peacebuilding is most sustainable when national actors define priorities and international partners align their resources, timelines, and accountability behind those priorities. Finally, partnerships are the channels through which trust is built and grievances are addressed early. Government institutions, civil society, faith-based actors, women, youth, traditional leaders, and development partners must therefore remain central to prevention, For Kenya, this means that locally-led peacebuilding should not be understood merely as the delivery of internationally financed projects by local organizations. Rather, local actors should have a voice, influence, institutional space, and access to resources. Mr. Chair, the future of peacebuilding will not be secured by building more projects around national institutions. It will be secured by strengthening the institutions through which societies prevent conflict, manage difference and build trust. At a time of shrinking resources, the choice before us is not between peace building and development. It is whether development investments will build societies resilient enough to withstand conflict or whether we will continue to meet the far greater cost of responding after crises have already occurred. Kenya believes the measure of our collective success must be practical. We stand ready to work with all partners in support of approaches that place national leadership and local agency at the center. Together, we can ensure that prevention is not only recognized as a priority, but embedded in the institutions, partnerships, and investments that shape our collective efforts to sustain peace. I thank you.

To address this, we are committed to promoting social cohesion by fostering mutual respect, unity, and inclusive governance, ensuring that all communities are heard and represented is essential in turning diversity into the foundation of national strength. Our Bougainville conflict left deep scars. For over a decade, civil war claimed approximately 20,000 lives. But through dialogue, perseverance, and a mutual respect, we chose peace by peaceful means over conflict. Our 2001 Bougainville Peace Agreement established a political roadmap under the confines of our country's constitution that witnessed unbroken peace in our country for 25 years. With the support of our development partners, including the United Nations, Peacebuilding Fund since 2015, we supported the Bougainville referendum and are now navigating the post-referendum transition. National prevention strategy 2025 to 2030. This was launched in September 25 in the presence of the UN Secretary General during his landmark visit to my country. This provides an important framework to address sources of conflict and promote inclusive and peaceful communities across the country. The National Provincial Strategy recognizes that conflict and violence prevention would be possible only through the collective engagement of businesses, churches, community leaders, civil society organizations, youth groups, and women organizations, and the whole of government approach and a whole of society approach and partnership where needed. Mr. Chair, addressing root causes is fundamental for peace and security. Conflicts today are increasingly interconnected with poverty, climate change, displacement, food and energy insecurity, weak institutions, organized crime and competition over natural resources. Where development is absent, grievances can deepen. Where institutions are weak, instability can take root. Where communities are excluded, social cohesion can fracture. And where young people see no economic future, the foundations of peace become fragile. For vulnerable countries, including small island development states, climate change presents another dimension of security and peace building. Rising sea levels, extreme weather events, disaster and loss of livelihoods can deepen existing vulnerabilities, increase displacement and place additional pressure on communities and institutions. This is why prevention must remain at the center of our collective approach to peace and security. We must invest in peace before crisis becomes conflicts. We must strengthen institutions before they fail. We must listen to communities before grievances become violence. And we must ensure that young people and women are not simply regarded as beneficiaries of peacebuilding, but as partners and leaders in building peace. Mr. Chair, international partners, including regional level corporations, have an important role to play in peacebuilding. in affected countries. However, external assistance cannot be a suitable for national ownership, sustainable for suitable national ownership. Papua New Guinea also believes that regional organizations and regional approaches deserve greater recognition. The experiences of the Pacific, demonstrate the value of dialogue, consensus, mediation, and locally grounded approaches to resolve differences. Our region has developed its own traditional and mechanisms for maintaining peace and security. They must compliment rather than compete with the global peace and security architecture. The international community is most effective when it supports nationally determined priorities, strengthens national institutions, and helps societies develop their own capacity to prevent and resolve conflict. In this spirit, the Peacebuilding Commission has an important role. in helping the United Nations systems move from a culture of responding to crisis towards a stronger culture of prevention, resilience, and sustained peace. Mr. Chair, let us therefore ensure that peacebuilding is not treated as a afterthought once conflict has occurred. Let us make sure it is an essential part of development, governments, and international cooperation. And let us build a peace-building system that is sufficiently flexible to listen to countries, sufficiently inclusive to hear communities, and sufficiently resourced to turn political commitments into lasting results. Our peacebuilding architecture must therefore be capable of connecting peace, development, human security, and resilience. Papua New Guinea stands ready to work with the United Nations, other member states, regional organizations, and the development partners to advance this shared objective. Because peace is not built in conference rooms alone. It is built in communities. It is built through trust. It is built through inclusion. And ultimately, it is built by the people who believe that their differences can be resolved without violence and that their children deserve a better future. Let us give them that future. And I thank you.

Peace endures when countries lead their own development path, supported by effective institutions, accountable governance, and inclusive participation that enables citizens, including the young people, the women, but also communities, to shape their own future. Investing earlier in resilience, institutions, and local capacities is not only more effective, it is also more cost efficient. than responding after crises have emerged. Our partnership with the United Nations Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office And I thank my dear sister, Elizabeth, for the wonderful work that we plan to do together.
